install_command: mkdir /tmp/qs && cd /tmp/qs && npm init -y && npm install fast-jev-compaction
quick_start: README 'Install and usage' snippet: compactMessages(transcript, { preserveRecentMessages: 4 }) then console.log(result.messages, result.decisions, result.stats) and reductionRatio(result). Run as plain ESM (node quickstart.mjs), with the '// …' part of the transcript filled in so it had 12 messages and 5 tool calls; key read from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (the project's default name).
result: One Jev request (471 ms, stateTokens 663, stage 'full'). Decisions: t1 Read keepCall 0.22/keepResult 0.12 drop_call; t2 Bash 0.20/0.12 drop_call; t3 Read 0.15/0.09 drop_call; t4 Edit and t5 Bash pinned. stats: messagesBefore 12 -> messagesAfter 6, charsBefore 10106 -> charsAfter 195, callsDropped 3, pinned 2, requests 1; reductionRatio 0.98.
beyond_readme: Had to create a project to install into (npm init -y). The package is ESM-only, so the script has to be .mjs or the project needs "type": "module".
The README example is TypeScript with an 'import type'. Running it needs tsx or tsc, which the README doesn't mention for library users. I used plain JS (.mjs) and dropped the type import.

The README transcript is incomplete ('// …'). As written it has 3 messages with preserveRecentMessages: 4, so every call is pinned and Jev would never be asked. I had to write extra messages (5 tool calls in total) to get a real Jev call.

Version mismatch: npm installs fast-jev-compaction 0.4.1, but the repo at ~/src is 0.2.0. The published package also ships files the repo doesn't have: cli/*.mjs, cli/jev-gate.py with a committed __pycache__ .pyc, SKILL.md, plugins/ and test dumps. So what users install is not the source in this checkout.

install_command: npx -y @jkudish/jev-mcp  (then, per the README's Claude Code section: claude mcp add jev -- npx -y @jkudish/jev-mcp; `claude mcp list` reports jev ✔ Connected)
quick_start: jev_verify, the README's first tool example: claims ["Wearing a helmet is optional for adult riders.", "The ordinance mentions reflective gear."] against the City Bicycle Safety Ordinance s.4 evidence text, called as tools/call over stdio to `npx -y @jkudish/jev-mcp` with TYPESAFE_API_KEY exported
result: model jev-1.13.0, provider typesafe; summary {verified:1, contradicted:1, unsupported:0, needs_review:0}; claim0 'helmet optional' -> contradicted (contradicts=1, confidence 1, action auto); claim1 'reflective gear' -> verified (supports=1, confidence 1, action auto); usage 891 input / 128 output tokens. Matches the README's 'live result, abridged'.
beyond_readme: The README has no standalone quick-start command: `npx -y @jkudish/jev-mcp` only starts a stdio server and waits for input, so I took the first tool example (jev_verify) as the quick start.

To actually call a tool without an LLM-driven MCP client session, I wrote a ~20-line Node stdio JSON-RPC client (initialize, notifications/initialized, tools/call). The README does not give a CLI or script for calling a tool directly.
The env var is already named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so I didn't need to rename it; I only had to `export` it so the spawned server inherits it.

beyond_readme: Skipped the README's first command ('agent start --agent codex'): it launches a separate host agent (Codex/Claude Code/Cursor) and asks for the key interactively. Ran the next example, 'Route one decision', which is the smallest one that calls Jev.

The 'Route one decision' example is only written for OpenRouter (OPENROUTER_API_KEY, --provider openrouter). To use the official TypeSafe key I swapped in '--provider typesafe'. That name comes from the README's 'Choose typesafe' prompt text and from src/cli.ts; no README example shows it as a CLI flag.
Cookbook 01 lists only OPENROUTER_API_KEY or JEV_API_KEY as prerequisites, but the README also accepts TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The key was already exported under that name, so nothing had to be renamed.
